statement: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that transforms a data matrix X of dimensions n x p into a lower-dimensional representation T = B * W of dimensions n x L (1 <= L <= p), where B = X - h * u^T is the mean-centered data matrix (with u_j = (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij} and h a vector of ones) and W consists of the first L columns of the eigenvector matrix V that diagonalizes the empirical covariance matrix C = (1/(n-1)) B^* B such that V^{-1} C V = D, with eigenvalues ordered decreasingly. Equivalently, for a random vector x, PCA seeks an orthonormal linear transformation y = B' x or y = W_L^T x that maximizes variance along orthogonal coordinates. The supplied sources genuinely contain no derivation of PCA: the expected derivation using Lagrange multipliers, quadratic form differentiation, or SVD factorization is entirely absent from the provided text, and the source section titled 'Derivation using the covariance method' is truncated and incomplete.

properties.property: Trace maximization: for any orthonormal transformation y = B' x (1 <= q <= p), tr(\Sigma_y) = tr(B' \Sigma B) is maximized by choosing B = A_q, the first q columns of eigenvector matrix A
properties.why: The leading q principal components capture the largest cumulative variance among all q-dimensional orthonormal linear projections

properties.property: Trace minimization: for orthonormal transformation y = B' x, tr(\Sigma_y) is minimized by choosing B = A_q^*, the last q columns of eigenvector matrix A
properties.why: The trailing principal components have minimal variance, enabling the detection of near-constant linear relationships between variables and outliers

properties.property: Spectral decomposition: the covariance matrix decomposes as \Sigma = \sum_{k=1}^p \lambda_k \alpha_k \alpha_k' with Var(x_j) = \sum_{k=1}^p \lambda_k \alpha_{kj}^2 under normalization \alpha_k' \alpha_k = 1
properties.why: The combined variance and entire covariance matrix decompose into decreasing contributions \lambda_k \alpha_k \alpha_k' from each principal component

properties.property: Covariance diagonalization: the eigenvector matrix V diagonalizes empirical covariance matrix C via V^{-1} C V = D, where D is diagonal
properties.why: Transforming data via V decorrelates all distinct components of the transformed variables

properties.property: Information-theoretic optimality under Gaussian noise: for signal model x = s + n with Gaussian signal s and i.i.d. Gaussian noise n, PCA projection y = W_L^T x maximizes mutual information I(y; s)
properties.why: PCA minimizes the upper bound on information loss I(x; s) - I(y; s) when noise is spherical Gaussian

properties.property: Centroid dominance elimination: uncentered covariance \Sigma_{unc} = n \mu \mu^T + (1/n) Z^T Z contains a rank-one term n \mu \mu^T that dominates the leading eigenvector unless mean subtraction is applied
properties.why: Subtracting empirical mean \mu removes the rank-one term so principal axes align with directions of maximal data variance

properties.property: Scale dependence: scaling variables by diagonal D = diag(\alpha_1, ..., \alpha_p) alters covariance to \Sigma^{(\alpha)} = D^T \Sigma D, rotating principal axes toward inflated-variance columns
properties.why: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues depend directly on measurement scales unless variables are standardized to unit variance or analyzed via correlation matrices

assumptions.assumption: The underlying structure and correlations among features are linear
assumptions.breaks_when: The true patterns or manifold in the dataset are non-linear, causing linear PCA to steer analysis away from true progress

assumptions.assumption: Variables have comparable measurement scales or have been normalized to unit variance
assumptions.breaks_when: Variables have different units or widely disparate scales, causing principal components to artificially align with inflated-variance features

assumptions.assumption: The data is mean-centered before calculating the covariance matrix
assumptions.breaks_when: Mean-centering is omitted on uncentered data, causing the rank-one term n \mu \mu^T to force the leading eigenvector toward the mean

assumptions.assumption: Data observations are free of unhandled serial correlation or autocorrelation structure
assumptions.breaks_when: Sample size is small (< 30 subjects/blocks) and data exhibits uncorrected serial correlation, biasing components beyond the first

assumptions.assumption: Centered signals can physically take negative values
assumptions.breaks_when: Domain signals are strictly non-negative (e.g., astrophysical exposures), where mean removal produces unphysical negative fluxes

assumptions.assumption: Additive noise components are independent, identically distributed, and Gaussian
assumptions.breaks_when: Noise components become dependent or correlated, causing PCA to lose its information-theoretic optimality

failure_modes.signature: The first principal component aligns almost completely with the variable possessing the largest numerical scale or arbitrary unit (e.g., Fahrenheit vs Celsius)
failure_modes.cause: Performing PCA on unstandardized covariance matrices of variables with disparate measurement units instead of standardizing to unit variance or using the correlation matrix

failure_modes.signature: The leading eigenvector points directly toward the data centroid \mu, obliterating variance structure in the centered data
failure_modes.cause: Failing to center the data before diagonalizing the covariance matrix, leaving the dominant rank-one term n \mu \mu^T in \Sigma_{unc}

failure_modes.signature: Reduced-dimension representations fail to identify key structures or obscure true data clusters
failure_modes.cause: Applying a strictly linear subspace projection to data governed by non-linear relationships

failure_modes.signature: Reconstructed signals or exposures exhibit negative fluxes
failure_modes.cause: Applying mean subtraction to strictly non-negative signals, forcing exposure means to zero

failure_modes.signature: Seriously biased eigenvectors and eigenvalues for principal components beyond the first
failure_modes.cause: Applying PCA to serially correlated data with fewer than 30 subjects or blocks without prior autocorrelation correction

failure_modes.signature: Overlapping classes and degraded classification accuracy in principal component space
failure_modes.cause: PCA optimizes for overall data variance rather than maximizing class separability
